stops.name: The Sabbath, preparing the spices
stops.campa: The Sabbath falls over Jerusalem like a held breath, and the law forbids all labor, even the labor of grief. Mary and the other women rest, as the commandment requires, and prepare what they can before sundown: the spices and ointments bought or set aside, kept ready for the one thing the law cannot forbid once the sun goes down a second time. She anointed his feet with nard while he lived; now she means to anoint the whole body in death, and the waiting through this one silent day is its own kind of vigil, spent in the house at Bethany among the mourning women.

stops.name: The Garden Tomb: the empty tomb, Easter morning
stops.campa: Very early, while it is yet dark, she comes to the tomb with spices and finds the stone already rolled away. She runs first, not to look inside, but to Peter and to the beloved disciple, with the only sentence she can form: they have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and she does not know where they have laid him. The men run back with her and find it just as she said, and go home again believing only that the body is gone. Mary stays behind, weeping at the mouth of an empty grave. She is the one who does not leave the garden.
stops.quote: They have taken away my Lord, and I know not where they have laid him.

stops.name: The Garden: Noli me tangere, apostle to the apostles
stops.campa: Weeping still, she turns and sees a man she takes for the gardener. Woman, why weepest thou? Whom seekest thou? She answers, still not knowing him. Then he speaks one word, her own name, Mary, and everything turns over at once. Rabboni, she cries, and reaches for him; he tells her not to hold him, for he is not yet ascended, but to go and tell his brethren. She runs to the eleven with the sentence the Church will never let go of: I have seen the Lord. The apostle to the apostles delivers the first Easter word ever spoken, to the men who are meant to be preaching it to her.
stops.quote: Rabboni... I have seen the Lord.

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Upper Room: Pentecost
stops.campa: In the upper room on Mount Zion, the same house where the bread was broken seven weeks before, Mary Magdalene continues with the eleven, with Jesus's mother, and with the other women in prayer, of one accord, waiting on the promise. When the day of Pentecost is fully come, the sound comes like a mighty rushing wind, and tongues of fire sit upon each of them, and they speak in tongues not their own. The apostle to the apostles receives the same fire as the apostles she once outran to the tomb: the Spirit, descending, does not ask who ran there first.

stops.name: Jerusalem: the persecution after Stephen, the scattering
stops.campa: Stephen is stoned outside the walls, and a great persecution rises against the young church at Jerusalem; Saul of Tarsus goes from house to house dragging out men and women. The company that gathered at Pentecost scatters into Judea, Samaria, and farther. Tradition holds that Mary Magdalene, with Lazarus and Martha her own household, and Maximin and others of the seventy-two disciples, are among those the authorities single out: too visible, too closely tied to the empty tomb and the risen Teacher, to be let go quietly. They are seized, and a harder road than any in Galilee opens ahead of them.

stops.name: Jaffa, cast to sea without oar, sail, or rudder
stops.campa: At the coast the persecutors put them into a ship without sail, oar, or rudder, meaning to drown a whole household of the new faith at once: Mary Magdalene, Lazarus, Martha, Maximin, Martha's chamberer Marcella, the blind man Cedonius whom Christ had healed from birth, and Sarah, an Egyptian handmaid attached to the company. They are pushed out onto open water with no means of steering and no means of returning. The sea that once fell still at a word from the Teacher is now asked, without a word from anyone aboard, to carry his friends home to it.

stops.name: Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer, the miraculous landing
stops.campa: Without oar or sail or any hand to steer it, the boat crosses the whole width of the sea and runs aground on a low shingle shore at the mouth of the Rhône, where the Camargue's salt flats meet the tide. The company comes ashore into a country whose language none of them speak, in the place the centuries will call Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer for the women who landed there. Sarah, the Egyptian servant, will be kept by the region's memory as patroness of all who wander without a country of their own. Her feast still gathers pilgrims to this same beach every May.

stops.name: Marseille: preaching to the pagans, the prince and princess's vow
stops.campa: In the old Greek port of Marseille, Mary Magdalene preaches to a people who sacrifice to idols, denouncing their worship with the same directness she once heard turned on her own sins. The prince who governs the city and his wife, childless and desperate, come to her by night; she tells them plainly that their gods can give them nothing, and that only the God whose empty tomb she witnessed can open a barren womb. The princess sees her three times in visions before the couple, still unconverted, strikes the bargain that will carry them across the sea to test the claim against Peter himself in Rome.

stops.name: The rock off Marseille: the storm, the princess's death
stops.campa: The prince and his pregnant wife take ship for Rome to put the Magdalene's word to Peter, and a violent storm catches them at sea. The princess goes into labor in the tempest, bears a son, and dies of the ordeal before the ship can make any harbor. The sailors, unwilling to keep two corpses and a living infant aboard, set the dead mother and the child ashore together on a bare rock and sail on without them, leaving the prince to weep over a wife he cannot bury and a son he cannot feed, on a stone in the middle of the open sea.

stops.name: Rome and Jerusalem, the prince's two years with Peter
stops.campa: The prince goes on to Rome alone and finds Peter, who confirms every word Mary Magdalene preached and takes him on to Jerusalem to walk the ground of the Passion and the empty tomb for two full years. All the while, on the rock where he left them, the dead woman's body lies uncorrupted and her infant son lives and thrives, nursed, the tradition insists, by the invisible care of the very saint whose word set this whole voyage in motion. The prince returns believing everything, not yet knowing how literally the promise of provision has been kept for him.

stops.name: The rock off Marseille: the return, the princess revived
stops.campa: Two years to the day, the ship passes the rock again and the prince finds his son alive and playing at the water's edge, kept whole by a power he cannot see. Falling to his knees he prays to the Magdalene by name to finish what she began: she who has fed and kept his son two years in this rock, let her restore also the boy's mother. The dead woman draws breath, opens her eyes, and rises as from ordinary sleep, telling of a pilgrimage of her own soul that ran, mile for mile, beside her husband's the whole two years, unseen by him.

stops.name: Marseille, the baptism of the prince and princess
stops.campa: The family returns rejoicing to Marseille and finds Lazarus, Mary Magdalene, and the rest of the company still at their preaching. The prince and princess destroy the idols of the city with their own hands and receive baptism from Maximin, becoming the first fruits of a Provence that will, in the centuries to come, count itself Christian from this very hour. Mary Magdalene, who arrived on a rudderless boat with nothing, now stands godmother to a whole converted household and, through them, to a coastline. Her preaching in the city complete, she turns her face toward the wilder country inland.
